intent: The mail hub's public boundary, frozen as language-neutral cases. This file is the contract; a driver is only one way to execute it. The Python driver (tests/mh01_contract.py) qualifies the pinned Python source; a second driver against the Rust binary qualifies the port with no change to this file.

conventions.principals: Symbolic names. The driver mints a fresh random slug and secret per principal per case, so no credential is ever written here.
conventions.placeholders: @<principal>.slug resolves to that principal's address; @cap.<name> to a value captured from an earlier response; @env.hub_name and @env.retention_days to the hub's configured identity.
conventions.as: Principals whose credentials go in X-Org-Auth, space separated. A ':bad' suffix presents a WRONG secret for that real slug. Omitted means no header at all.
conventions.surface: 'full' is the whole app; 'public' is the FR-10 API-only listener. Coverage accounting uses the full surface only.
conventions.legacy: true marks behaviour recorded as it IS, not as v3 wants it. A port must reproduce it or carry a recorded ruling to change it -- it must not be silently 'fixed'.
conventions.store: Two seams a wire profile cannot express: backdating a row, and running one retention pass. Any driver must provide both.

cases.intent: A first registration mints the address and answers with the hub's identity, its retention policy and the full roster.
The roster row a client sees is slug/org_name/username/blurb/online/last_seen/kind. Default kind is 'org'.
FR-06: an independent chat session registers as kind 'chat'; anything other than the exact string 'chat' falls back to 'org'.
The slug grammar is ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,127}$. Uppercase, spaces and a leading separator are all refused.
Registration authenticates INLINE rather than through the shared helper: the header must carry a secret for the very slug being registered. No header, or a header for a different slug, is refused.
Joining is open but ADDRESSES are owned. Once a slug is held, a different secret is refused 403 -- taking it requires producing a secret that hashes to the holder's stored fingerprint.
The same secret re-registering is not an error: it updates org_name/username/blurb and keeps the address.
The polite exit removes only the caller's own roster rows and names them back.
An unauthenticated caller cannot remove anyone.
A wrong secret for a real slug does not authenticate. This is the address-theft attempt in its cheapest form; the hub compares the FULL sha256 digest, never the 6-character display suffix.
A header with no colon, an empty slug or an empty secret contributes no principal, so the call is refused rather than partially trusted.
A never-registered slug is simply not a principal.
One call may carry several identities. Invalid pairs drop out of the principal set; the call proceeds for the valid ones rather than failing whole.
The roster is not public on the API surface.
The 200 IS the 'received' receipt: it confirms hub custody and returns the id, the hub-clock received_at and whether this was a duplicate.

The envelope a recipient sees is exactly id/from/to/body/kind/thread_id/sent_at/received_at/attachments. `sent_at` is the sender's claim and rides through untouched; `received_at` is the hub clock and is the ordering authority.
A sender must present credentials, and the `from` it claims must be one of them.
Presenting alpha's credentials while claiming to be beta is refused: `from` must be inside the authenticated set.
The hub refuses mail to an address nobody holds, rather than queueing for a stranger.
BODY_MAX mirrors the org-inbox truncation. An over-long body is TRUNCATED and accepted, not refused -- the port must not turn this into an error.

The message id is client-minted and the insert is INSERT OR IGNORE, so a retry is idempotent: the second call reports duplicate:true, returns the ORIGINAL received_at, and the stored body stays the first one.
cases.legacy_note: This is NOT the approved v3 original-key replay contract. A same-id send with a CHANGED payload is silently accepted as a duplicate rather than refused as a conflict, and the changed body is discarded without telling the sender. Recorded as it is; a port must not quietly bless it as the target semantics, and must not quietly fix it either -- changing it needs a recorded ruling.

cases.intent: MAX_FILES_PER_MESSAGE is 10 and is checked before any attachment is resolved.
An attachment id must exist AND be owned by the sender. A stranger's blob cannot be attached to your mail.
Polling is authenticated; there is no anonymous drain.
received_at then rowid is the ordering authority -- NOT the sender's claimed sent_at. Here sent_at is deliberately reversed and the delivery order must still follow the hub clock.
Delivery is at-least-once. A message stays queued -- and keeps coming back on every poll -- until the recipient acknowledges custody. Collapsing the repeat is the client's job.
The sender acknowledging its own message must be a no-op. Custody belongs to the addressee.
Only the queued->fetched transition counts. A repeated ack is accepted and reports 0, so a retrying client cannot inflate custody.
There is no anonymous acknowledgment.
One instance holds several orgs and polls once for all of them. Mail for each presented identity arrives in the same response.
The recipient reports delivered, then read; the sender collects both on its own poll. 'fetched' comes from the ack, 'delivered' and 'read' from the recipient's receipts.
A receipt is marked pushed when it is returned, so the sender's NEXT poll does not repeat it. This is loss-tolerant by design: a dropped response loses display state, never a message.
The timestamp column is set only while NULL, so a second 'delivered' records 0 -- the ladder is monotonic. A third party cannot report on someone else's mail.
Only 'delivered' and 'read' are recorded. Anything else is skipped silently and counts 0 -- the call still succeeds.
Receipt reporting is authenticated.
The uploader gets back a server-minted id and the byte count actually stored. The filename arrives as a query parameter and is basename-d and capped at 255 characters.
Anonymous blob upload is refused; the first presented principal becomes the owner.
MAX_FILE_BYTES is 25 MiB and mirrors the orgtree caps. One byte over is refused with 413, not truncated.
Before any send binds it, only the owner can fetch the blob.
Binding an attachment to a message extends read rights to that message's addressee -- and to nobody else.
The recipient learns id/name/bytes with the message itself, so it never has to be told out of band that files exist.
An id nobody minted is 404 -- distinct from 403 for a real blob you may not read.
Even a correct id is refused without credentials.
Metadata outliving its bytes is reported as 410 gone, not as a 404 or an empty 200. The retention sweep removes file and row together, so this is the torn-state answer.
healthz is unauthenticated and is what a host readiness probe consumes: ok, the hub name, the org count, the queued count and the retention policy.

RULED, not a defect: on a closed network hub access IS read access to all mail, so the read-only view at / carries no credential check. A port must keep it unauthenticated AND keep it off the public listener.
/ui/data is the roster plus a per-org queued count, unauthenticated.
The operator page sorts received_at DESC, rowid DESC -- the reverse of delivery order -- and rides `n` (the rowid) out on every row for the cursor.
(before_at, before_n) is a keyset cursor in the SAME order the page sorts by, so paging stays stable while new mail keeps arriving. An OFFSET would skip or duplicate rows whenever the head moved.
A caller cannot ask the operator page for an unbounded read, and cannot ask for nothing either.

The UI groups by the REGISTERED username while the slug's middle segment is the sanitized one -- identical for orgs, diverging for chats (raw ncola_k8bx vs slug ncola-k8bx). Neither key is ever rewritten; both are folded on case and _/- for the comparison.
Beyond the envelope, the operator view adds state, delivered_at, read_at and n. `n` is the rowid and is the cursor identity a migration must not lose.
FR-10: the public listener is a route split, not a blind tunnel. Every /api/* route is gated on the caller's own secret, so those plus /healthz are exactly what a remote client needs.
Tunnelling the full port would publish the unauthenticated all-mail UI. The public face must 404 the operator routes -- this is the security boundary, not cosmetics.
Past HUB_RETENTION_DAYS a message, its attachment row and the blob file all go. Mail inside the window is untouched. Retention is the hub's only forgetting mechanism for messages.
Roster hygiene ages out a client unseen for HUB_ORG_RETENTION_DAYS -- EXCEPT one that still holds queued mail. Never strand a delivery.
